topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: A benchmark is an experiment whose result depends on its workload and measurement boundary. The question is not whether a number looks small, but whether two implementations were asked to perform equivalent work under comparable conditions. This chapter compares two reductions, preserves a correctness checksum, and reports repeated timings without asserting that either implementation must win.

topics.title: 12.1.1 Preventing Compiler Elimination
topics.summary: The compiler is allowed to remove work whose result cannot affect observable behavior. Consume the result in a way the compiler must preserve and provide inputs that represent runtime work. Merely placing a timer around a pure expression does not guarantee the intended instructions remain.

topics.title: 12.1.2 Measuring Repeated Operations
topics.summary: Very short operations can be smaller than timer overhead or resolution. Measure a batch, repeat independent samples, and report the batch definition. Separate setup costs only when the real workload also amortizes them; otherwise excluding allocation or conversion answers a different question from end-to-end performance.

topics.title: 12.2.1 Understanding Variance
topics.summary: Variation is information about the experiment. Report multiple samples and a summary such as a median, while retaining the raw values for investigation. An isolated minimum can approximate an uncontended case but does not describe tail latency experienced by users.

topics.title: Trace the implementation
topics.summary: Both functions sum the same bounded integer data into long long. The four-lane version maintains independent accumulators before combining them and handles the remaining tail explicitly. The input length is intentionally not a multiple of four, so an implementation that ignores the tail fails the comparison.
